# Can AI Make Its Own Manufacturing Decisions?

AI can optimize processes and find defects, but autonomous decisions require better data and strict process controls.

Key Takeaways:

- AI can identify promising process conditions and recognize manufacturing problems, but those results still require physical validation before they can be trusted in production.

- Incomplete manufacturing data and uncertainty about downstream effects make it difficult to give AI systems authority over process adjustments.

- Greater manufacturing autonomy will require clear decision boundaries, failure containment, and ways to qualify models that change as they learn.

Semiconductor manufacturing has always depended on engineers making decisions involving complex interactions among process parameters. An etch recipe, for example, may involve combinations of RF power, pressure, gas chemistry, temperature, and timing, each affecting multiple process characteristics. Changing one parameter might improve critical dimension control while creating problems elsewhere. But as devices and manufacturing processes become more complicated, the growing number of variables involved makes those decisions increasingly difficult.

AI-driven manufacturing offers a way to manage some of that complexity, from finding better process conditions to identifying defects and responding to problems on the production line. But how much production responsibility engineers are willing to give those systems remains an open question, and one that drew considerable attention at SEMICON West 2026.

“No matter how good we are as engineers, no matter how disciplined and objective we are, we tend to approach these difficult problems with historical biases,” said David Fried, chief AI officer and corporate vice president of Semiverse Solutions at Lam Research during a conference panel. “A process engineer might look at a set of data and say, ‘I need to move into a lower-pressure, higher-power regime because that’s how we solved this problem 10 years ago.’ But with this massive parameter space, AI can point us in a different direction, into an operating region we might never have considered because we couldn’t see those relationships in the data before.”

Finding a process that keeps working Finding an unfamiliar operating condition is useful, but determining whether it will hold up in production is another matter. Two recipes may produce similar results during development, yet respond quite differently to changes in incoming materials or equipment conditions. AI can help engineers identify those differences before committing to a particular process.

“It’s not just a question of delivering to a particular performance point. It’s also a question of how stable that particular performance point is, how robust it is,” said Vikas Sharma, senior principal engineer and senior director of pathfinding for Intel Foundry R&D, in a recent presentation. “Minor perturbations in the incoming material or at the tool can lead to a significant drop in performance.”

The scale of the optimization problem helps explain why AI-driven manufacturing is attracting so much interest. Fried described a current Lam Research etcher with a potential recipe space on the order of 10²³ combinations. At Intel, Sharma discussed a process involving 350 parameters and approximately 10⁷⁰⁰ theoretical combinations.

According to Sharma, engineers working with equipment suppliers spent about a year developing a minimally acceptable recipe for that particular tool and process layer, followed by an extended effort to improve it with limited success. After introducing AI-assisted optimization, they began finding better results within a few months, eventually identifying multiple solutions that improved on the original baseline.

The challenge was determining which solutions were worth pursuing. Sharma noted that AI could identify thousands of candidates, but evaluating them still required expensive silicon experiments. Engineers also had to account for nonlinear relationships among parameters, which could change considerably across different operating regions.

“AI is not a magic wand. You can’t use the same AI solution for every problem,” Fried said. “Figuring out whether you’re using full physical simulation, surrogate models, machine learning, deep learning, LLM-based AI, or agentic AI, which of these solutions you’re building in which form to solve which problem and address which workflow, that’s more of what we’re spending our time on than actually building it or implementing it.”

The different approaches serve different purposes, from exploring process conditions to coordinating engineering workflows. Combining them may allow engineers to investigate more possibilities, but it also raises questions about how the results should be validated and whether the assumptions used in one model remain appropriate when its recommendations are passed to another.

When the factory acts on what it sees Inspection is one of the more established applications of AI in manufacturing, particularly in advanced packaging, where finer pitches and more complicated structures have increased the number of connections that must be examined. Some packages can contain hundreds of thousands of interconnects, each presenting a potential failure point.

Automated optical inspection and X-ray systems collect extensive information about those structures. Machine learning can identify variations that might be difficult to distinguish visually, but manufacturers still need to determine which differences indicate actual defects.

“When we look at X-rays, everybody just sees all shades of gray, but AI can see a thousand shades of gray,” said Ingu Yin Chang, executive vice president at ASE Group . “But the AI only knows if this shade of gray equates to a problem once we say, ‘Hey, this equates to a problem.’ So, you’ve got to have the physical data that says, ‘Okay, that is a problem.’ Then, in the future, they can scan for that shade of gray and that location.”

Once manufacturers determine which image characteristics correspond to actual defects, AI-enabled inspection systems can flag abnormalities during production and trigger predefined equipment responses. At ASE, systems can recognize known abnormalities and trigger equipment responses before additional assemblies are affected.

“We have figured out how to do a lot of automation and use AI to help us identify potential issues, based on the issues that we physically learned through traditional manufacturing methods,” Chang said. “We will know when a wire bond is not bonded correctly, and the machine will immediately stop. There’s constant AI oversight to ask, ‘Are we doing everything correctly? Are we seeing it as we planned to see it?’”

Stopping equipment when a defect is detected can prevent additional losses, but it doesn’t necessarily mean AI is controlling the process independently. The inspection system may identify an abnormal condition while a conventional controller executes a predefined response. Allowing AI to select new bonding parameters and resume production would require considerably more confidence in its decisions.

ASE’s product diversity makes that challenge more difficult. Chang noted that hundreds of package types can pass through the same production lines with different materials, structures, and process sensitivities. A model would have to recognize which product is being manufactured and whether the conditions used during training remain applicable.

An inspection system might correctly identify a defective bond, but changing the process to prevent another failure requires knowing what caused it and whether an adjustment will create problems elsewhere. Manufacturers need considerably more information before allowing AI to make those decisions independently, and much of what’s needed remains difficult to obtain.

Proving the model is right One of the first obstacles to AI-driven manufacturing is establishing whether an AI recommendation accurately represents the physical process. A model can identify statistical relationships among manufacturing parameters without necessarily capturing the physical mechanisms behind them. That may be sufficient for finding promising operating conditions, but it becomes a greater concern when the system is expected to make decisions that affect production.

Sharma’s Intel example illustrates the problem. Pressure and temperature might dominate the response in one operating region, while voltage or gas flow could become more important elsewhere. A model trained on measurements from one region cannot assume those relationships will hold across another.

“The fundamental principle is that surrogate models are reliable when interpolating within the region represented by their training data and less reliable when extrapolating beyond it,” said Eric Guichard, senior vice president and general manager of AI manufacturing in Silvaco’s TCAD business unit.

Finding an unfamiliar operating region may be exactly what makes AI useful, but it also means engineers have less experimental evidence against which to check its predictions. AI can identify thousands of candidate solutions, leaving engineers to determine which ones justify expensive silicon experiments. Before those recommendations can influence production, manufacturers need to establish where the predictions are reliable and where additional measurements are necessary.

Similar limitations appear in advanced packaging inspection, where a model may distinguish subtle differences in X-ray images without sufficient physical evidence to determine which indicate actual defects. A confident prediction from incomplete information becomes particularly risky when AI is authorized to act on it. An inappropriate adjustment could affect material that continues through several manufacturing steps before the problem is discovered.

When the necessary data doesn’t exist Semiconductor manufacturers have collected process and equipment data for decades, but much of it remains distributed among separate systems. Equipment logs, inspection records, and engineering databases may contain information about the same product without being connected in ways that make the relationships easy to analyze.
